title: Music Before Writing
description: Ice Age flutes, a contested Neanderthal flute and the oldest instruments still played

concepts.title: The Vulture-Bone Flute
concepts.contentHtml:
You do not need to read music to begin this story, because for almost all of human history nobody could. The oldest music that survives is not written down at all: it is objects. In 2008 a team led by the archaeologist Nicholas Conard of the University of Tübingen found the pieces of a flute at1 Hohle Fels, a Stone Age cave in southern Germany. It was made from the naturally hollow wing bone of a griffon vulture, only 8 millimetres wide and originally about 34 centimetres long, with five finger holes and a V-shaped mouthpiece.

Nearby lay fragments of flutes carved from mammoth ivory, and these are the real surprise. Ivory is solid. Using only stone tools, the maker had to split a section of curved ivory along its natural grain, hollow out and carve the two halves, then fit them back together with an airtight seal.2 Someone went to enormous trouble to make a tube that plays notes.

How old are they? Here you meet the first rule of musical archaeology: you rarely date the instrument itself. Researchers radiocarbon-dated animal bones found in the same layer as flutes from the nearby cave of3 Geissenklösterle, and in 2012 reported ages of 42,000 to 43,000 years.4 That is a date for the layer, so it is only as good as the link between the bones and the flutes. Conard read the results as support for the idea that the River Danube was a corridor for people and new technologies moving into central Europe between 40,000 and 45,000 years ago.

The vulture flute comes from the same cave as the Venus of Hohle Fels, the ivory figurine you met in Art History. Conard said the new flutes date to the very period when modern humans settled the region. Music did not arrive late, once life became comfortable: it came with the first settlers.

concepts.title: A Flute, or a Hyena's Leftovers?
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1995 Ivan Turk and Janez Dirjec of the Slovenian Institute of Archaeology were excavating the cave of1 Divje Babe in Slovenia when they found the thigh bone of a young cave bear pierced by a row of holes. It lay in a layer linked to Neanderthals. If it was a flute, it was the oldest instrument in the world and proof that Neanderthals made music. Slovenia's official portal still presents it that way: a bone found near a Neanderthal fire pit 50,000 to 60,000 years old, now displayed in the National Museum of Slovenia in Ljubljana.

Now look at it as a specialist in animal bones would. In 2015 the researcher Cajus Diedrich compared it with cave-bear bones from dens across Europe. His verdict was blunt: these bones are not instruments, nor human made, but the work of hyenas.2 Ice Age spotted hyenas scavenged bear cubs in their dens. A cub's thigh bone is only lightly calcified, so when a hyena's bone-crushing premolars bit down, they often punched round or oval holes instead of shattering it, sometimes on both sides of the shaft. X-rays showed no drill scratches or stone-tool marks around the holes.3

Diedrich also attacks the context. He argues that the cave's archaeology belongs to modern humans, not Neanderthals, and that the only absolute date, about 43,000 years, was measured on the bone itself.4 One supporter of the flute, Fink, had claimed that the spacing of the holes matched a diatonic scale, the seven-note do-re-mi pattern. Diedrich replies that a whole wave of supposed cave-bear bone instruments followed, based solely on holes in bones.

The debate is still open, and Turk's team has published new studies defending the flute. Notice what it teaches: every claimed instrument must first pass one test. Can nature, here a hungry hyena, explain the holes just as well?

concepts.title: Blowing Into the Past
concepts.contentHtml:
Some ancient instruments can still be played. At Jiahu, an early Neolithic village in Henan province, China, excavators found six complete bone flutes between 7,000 and 9,000 years old.1 The site was inhabited from 7000 to 5700 BCE. The flutes were all made from the wing bones of the red-crowned crane and have five, six, seven or eight holes.2 A 1999 press release from Brookhaven National Laboratory, whose chemist Garman Harbottle helped date the site, called them possibly the earliest complete, playable, tightly dated instruments that could sound several notes. Tonal analysis suggested that the seven holes of one flute gave a scale strikingly like the Western do-re-mi.

Older still is a seashell. In 1931 excavators at the decorated cave of Marsoulas in France found a large conch. Its finders saw no trace of human work and interpreted it as a "loving cup".3 A team led by Carole Fritz looked again and published the results in 2021. The tip of the shell had been removed and pierced inside, brownish residue suggested a mouthpiece had been fixed there, and red dots the size of fingerprints decorated the inside. The cave's layers date to about 18,000 years ago, and the shell is kept in the collection of the Natural History Museum of Toulouse.4

Then a horn player blew it. The shell sounded three notes, at about 256, 265 and 285 vibrations per second (hertz), each roughly a semitone apart:5 the smallest step between neighbouring keys on a piano. It was loud too, about 100 decibels at a metre. It was the first time anyone had heard it in some 18,000 years.

But notice what is still missing: the tunes. Instruments tell you which notes were possible. Without writing, the music itself is gone. That is why the next lesson starts with clay tablets.

title: The First Written Music
description: Babylonian tuning tablets, Greek songs in stone and China's two-tone bells

concepts.title: Lyres of Ur and the Tuning Tablets
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest stringed instruments known from ancient Sumer and Babylonia come from the Royal Cemetery of Ur in ancient Iraq. Without the eleven stringed instruments recovered at Ur, two harps and nine lyres, we would not have a single actual stringed instrument from that world.1 Their wood has long gone, but their gold, silver, copper, lapis lazuli and shell decoration survived in the earth. The large Bull-Headed Lyre, with its long strings, would have sounded something like a bass viol, a deep bowed instrument; a medium-sized silver lyre now in the British Museum might have sounded like a cello.

Instruments show which notes were possible; writing shows how people thought about them. Since 1959 scholars have recognised a small number of cuneiform tablets about tuning and playing instruments. They share a standard set of Akkadian terms for the strings, for intervals (the distance between two notes) such as fifths and fourths, and for seven named scales. A fifth is the interval whose frequencies stand in the ratio 3:2, which the Pythagoreans later made famous (you met them in Philosophy of Mathematics).

A tuning text from Ur gives explicit instructions as to which strings to tighten or loosen to tune each of the seven scales.2 The Assyriologist Anne Draffkorn Kilmer concluded that by about 1800 BCE Babylonian musicians used a seven-note, diatonic system of seven interrelated scales, and that one of them was equivalent to the modern major scale. Many scholars found that hard to believe.

The system also travelled: the same Akkadian terms appear in instructions to performers of Hurrian cult hymns at Ugarit, a trading city on the Syrian coast that collapsed in the twelfth century BCE.3 Yet Kilmer herself warned against over-reading. When people hear a reconstruction, they often say it sounds too Western to be right.4 Her answer was that there is no evidence that ancient Near Eastern music sounded like modern Near Eastern music either. We have the intervals and the tunings, not the performance.

concepts.title: Greek Songs in Stone
concepts.contentHtml:
For the ancient Greeks, mousike covered not only music but also dance, lyrics and the performance of poetry. Each instrument had a divine inventor: Hermes the lyre, Pan the panpipes, Athena the aulos, a pipe usually played in pairs. In Athens in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, schools of music taught pupils aged between 13 and 16 to play the lyre and the kithara, a larger lyre, and to sing.1 The Greeks also believed that music shaped character, which is why Plato, thinking them decadent, banned instruments capable of producing all of the scales.

Theory was taken seriously. The followers of Pythagoras treated music as a mathematical expression of the cosmic order, and the earliest surviving text on the subject, the Harmonic Elements of Aristoxenus, was written in the 4th century BCE. The Greeks wrote melodies down too, but only fragments survive: about 52 pieces of Greek music, including an excerpt from Euripides' play2 Orestes and music inscribed at the Athenian Treasury at Delphi. The most complete surviving piece is the song of Seikilos, carved on a tombstone found at Tralleis near Ephesus.

Now a famous myth: Nero fiddled while Rome burned. When the Great Fire began on the evening of 18 July 64 CE, Nero was at his seaside villa and did not return until the flames threatened his own palace. A rumour soon spread that he had played his lyre and sung about the burning of Troy while his city burned.3 The fiddle was added to the story later, since fiddles were not invented until the 16th century.4

Why did the rumour stick? Because it fitted. Nero really did love singing and playing the lyre, and he often acted in tragedies, performing roles such as Hercules and Oedipus. An emperor who sang on stage made an easy target.

concepts.title: The Bells of Marquis Yi
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 433 BCE a local ruler of the state of Zeng in central China, Marquis Yi, was buried with a lavish collection of musical instruments. His tomb filled with water, which preserved the contents in excellent condition.1 In Suizhou, in Hubei province, archaeologists recovered a set of 65 bronze chime bells weighing nearly 5 tonnes, the bianzhong. The bells are now on display in the Hubei Provincial Museum in Wuhan.

The surprise is in their shape. Most of these ancient Chinese bells are oval or almond-shaped in cross-section, not round, so each one sounds two distinctly different tones depending on where it is struck.2 Inscriptions on the bells name the intended interval between the two tones: a major third or a minor third, in Western terms. A major third is the gap from do to mi; a minor third is a semitone narrower.

Acousticians measure intervals in cents, where a full octave is 1,200 cents, a minor third about 300 and a major third about 400. When the physicist Thomas Rossing and colleagues measured all 65 bells, the gaps clustered around those two values but spread from about 210 to 490 cents.3 They found that the intervals did not track the obvious physical features of the bells, so nobody yet knows exactly how the founders controlled them.

The bells also carry 3,755 inscribed Chinese characters, described as the only known systematic musical treatise from the 5th century BCE.4 So here the instruments carry their own theory, and they still sound. On 1 August 1978 the bells gave their first modern performance, and in 2025 they were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

title: Writing It Down: Chant, Staff and Song
description: How chant got its name and its notation, Guido's staff and ut-re-mi, Hildegard and the troubadours

concepts.title: Gregorian Chant Before Gregory
concepts.contentHtml:
The traditional single-line chant of the Latin church carries a pope's name: Gregorian chant, after Pope Gregory the Great (590 to 604). For a long time, general histories of music assumed that the chant dated back to at least the 6th century and that Gregory put it in its present form.1 The evidence tells a different story. The first manuscripts containing Gregorian chant date from the 9th century and come from the Frankish empire, not from Rome.2

Many of those manuscripts open with a verse praising a Gregory. One scholar calls it a kind of Carolingian publicity technique, a way to advertise that the new chants were in the Roman style.3 It cannot be proved that the Gregory meant is Gregory the Great rather than Gregory II (715 to 731). The view associated with the musicologist Apel is that the Roman chant of Charlemagne's time combined with the Gallican chant of the Franks during the 8th century to give birth to the version now called Gregorian. What Gregory the Great certainly did was bring order to the texts of the liturgy.

Why write chant down at all? Because the repertoire for Mass and the daily services at the beginning of the 9th century must have comprised well over 2,000 pieces, and until then all of it had to be held in memory. Teaching it to each new generation of monks and cantors was an ever-increasing burden.

The first notation, signs now called neumes, merely indicated the direction the melody was to take, up or down, without accurate pitch differences.4 Think of it as a set of reminders for someone who already knew the tune: very useful for remembering, almost useless for learning a melody you had never heard. Solving that problem is the subject of the next concept.

concepts.title: Guido's Staff and Ut-Re-Mi
concepts.contentHtml:
Guido of Arezzo was a Benedictine monk who studied at the abbey of Pomposa, near Ferrara, and then taught singing there. At Pomposa he developed a new way of writing Gregorian chant, adopting a four-line staff and clefs,1 so that the height of a note on the page fixed its pitch. His ideas met with little understanding, and around 1025 he left the abbey for Arezzo, where he trained singers for the cathedral. During the 1020s he rewrote a volume of chants in his new notation and presented it to Pope John XIX, who was greatly impressed.2

His second invention was for the ear. Guido took a well-known 8th-century hymn for the feast of St John the Baptist and gave it a melody in which the first notes of the first six lines rise step by step. The Latin syllables that begin those lines, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, became names for the six notes, a pattern of two whole tones, a half tone and two whole tones called a hexachord. A singer who knew the hymn could find any interval by recalling which line began on which note. This system, known as solmization, became the basis of modern solfeggio, the do-re-mi of singing lessons.

Reference works disagree about the details, which is normal for an 11th-century life. One dates his textbook, the Micrologus, to about 1030; another gives 1025. One calls Guido the inventor of the Guidonian hand, a memory aid with note names placed on the joints and tips of the fingers; another says Guido or one of his disciples invented it.3

What is not in doubt is the effect. His innovations trained singers to learn new chants quickly,4 and notation changed its job: it could now teach a melody that nobody in the room had heard, instead of only reminding singers of one they already knew.

concepts.title: Hildegard, and Songs Outside the Church
concepts.contentHtml:
Hildegard of Bingen (c. 1098 to 1179) was a Benedictine abbess, mystic and composer who became famous in her own lifetime for her visions, writings and music. You met her invented language in Constructed Languages. As a girl she was taught to play the psaltery, a stringed instrument like a zither.1 She believed that before the Fall humans worshipped God with celestial song, and that music was the best expression of love for and devotion to God.

Her Ordo Virtutum ("Order of the Virtues"), completed in 1151, is described as the oldest medieval morality play, a sung drama about a soul torn between the Virtues and the Devil. Hildegard and her nuns sang the Virtues and the Soul, and male clergy sang the patriarchs and prophets. One character does not sing at all. Satan, probably played by the monk Volmar who had encouraged her to write, only speaks, because for Hildegard the Devil is incapable of producing music, the true praise of God.2

Music also lived far from the cloister. From the 11th century, poets in the south of France called troubadours composed and sang lyrics about love and chivalry in Provençal, the langue d'oc. Much of their work survives in songbooks, and it was highly influential in the development of European lyric poetry.3 Dictionaries disagree on when the tradition ended, putting it in the 13th or the 14th century.

Notice whose music survives. Chant, Hildegard's songs and troubadour lyrics were written down by and for people who could read. The work songs and dances of ordinary people were rarely written down, so we know far less about them: the written record preserves what literate people valued, not what most people sang.

title: Print, Tuning and the Birth of Opera
description: Music printing, the long argument over tuning and pitch, and how opera began

concepts.title: Music Goes to Press
concepts.contentHtml:
Before printing, every copy of a piece of music was written out by hand. On 25 May 1498 the Venetian Senate granted Ottaviano Petrucci a twenty-year patent for printing polyphonic music with movable type,1 the first known record of a privilege granted for music printing. Polyphony means several independent melodic lines sounding at once, like four people singing different tunes that fit together. In 1501 Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, an anthology of 96 secular songs, mostly French chansons, for three or four voices.

Printing notes is harder than printing words, because each note must sit exactly on its line. Petrucci ran each sheet through the press more than once: when he printed music with words, he used three impressions, first for the staffs, second for the notes and third for the lyrics.2 He laid out two parts on each side of an opening so that four singers or players could read from the same book.

Print also created records, and records let historians test legends. Take Greensleeves, often credited to Henry VIII, supposedly for Anne Boleyn. The earliest trace of the song is an entry in the register of the Stationers' Company in London: on 3 September 1580 Richard Jones registered a ballad called3 "A newe northen Dittye of ye Ladye Green Sleves". The first surviving printing of the words dates from 1584, and the tune itself first appears in 1652.4

So the song belongs to the reign of Elizabeth I, and it is traced to an Italian song form called the romanesca. Henry VIII was a reasonably skilled performer who did some composing, but as one ballad scholar puts it, there is little sign that he had the skill to write such a tune.5 The legend is attractive; the paperwork points elsewhere.

concepts.title: Tuning Wars: Temperament and Pitch
concepts.contentHtml:
Western tuning hides a mathematical snag. Tune twelve pure fifths in a row, each in the ratio 3:2, and you overshoot seven octaves by a small amount, so the circle never quite closes. Every tuning is therefore a compromise. Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal semitones. Its fifths are slightly smaller than pure ones, not enough to bother most listeners, but enough to make every half-step the same size and let a piece change key freely.1

Before equal temperament, the commonest system was meantone, which made certain keys sound sweet, others less so, and some unusable. When did equal temperament take over? Here the sources disagree. One standard reference says that equal temperament is the meaning of "well-tempered" in the title of Bach's2 Well-Tempered Clavier, his preludes and fugues in every major and minor key. Another, the Concise Oxford Dictionary of Music, says equal temperament was introduced for pianos in England in 1846.3 If most keyboards used other tunings until then, was Bach's tuning equal at all? The title alone cannot settle it.

Pitch itself also wandered. There was no universally accepted standard: records show the A that musicians tuned to varied across Europe from 409 to 457 vibrations per second (hertz).4 A tuning fork kept for Mozart by the piano builder Johann Andreas Stein sounded A at 421.6 Hz.5 The French government adopted 435 Hz in 1859, and at a conference in London in May 1939 delegates unanimously agreed to recommend 440 Hz.6

You may have seen claims online that 432 Hz is the natural, ancient pitch, that Mozart used it, and that the Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels imposed 440. A fact-check found these claims baseless. Of 85 historical pitch samples recorded by the Victorian scholar Alexander Ellis, not one measures exactly 432 Hz.7

concepts.title: The Invention of Opera
concepts.contentHtml:
Opera began as an experiment by learned amateurs. In the 1580s a circle of Florentine musicians and thinkers, the Camerata, met at the home of Count Giovanni de' Bardi, and their interest in reviving elements of ancient Greek drama led to a new kind of music drama. The composer Jacopo Peri probably took part. In the 1590s Peri and Jacopo Corsi set Ottavio Rinuccini's pastoral Dafne to music, and its first known performance was a private one in Florence in 1598.1

Dafne is generally recognised as the first opera in the new monodic style: solo voices supported by instruments, singing a flexible, speech-like line called recitative. Peri's next opera, Euridice, again to Rinuccini's words, was given at the Palazzo Pitti in Florence on 6 October 1600 for the wedding of Maria de' Medici and Henri IV of France.2 Some of its music was rewritten for that first performance by another composer, Giulio Caccini.

Then came a composer of genius. Claudio Monteverdi, in the service of the Gonzaga dukes of Mantua, wrote L'Orfeo, a "fable in music" first given before the Accademia degli Invaghiti in Mantua in February 1607. It has long been considered the first great opera.3 Its libretto was influenced by Rinuccini's Euridice, which tells the same myth of Orpheus.

So far opera was a court luxury, staged for weddings and academies. That changed in 1637, when the first public opera houses opened in Venice.4 Opera now had a public audience as well as princely patrons, and Monteverdi found a new outlet there for his productions.

title: The Age of the Composer
description: Bach's day job, Mozart's myths and Beethoven's hearing, tested against the evidence

concepts.title: Bach, the Third Choice
concepts.contentHtml:
We tend to picture great composers as free spirits. Johann Sebastian Bach was an employee, moving from post to post as an organist and court musician. In 1705 he obtained leave to travel to Lübeck to hear the famous organist Dietrich Buxtehude, presumably hoping to succeed him. The job came with a peculiar clause: Buxtehude had five unmarried daughters, and his successor was expected to marry the eldest.1 Bach became organist at Mühlhausen in June 1707 and a year later court organist to Duke Wilhelm Ernst of Weimar.

His most famous post came grudgingly. When Johann Kuhnau, the cantor of Leipzig, died in June 1722, Bach applied for his post, but the city authorities offered it first to Telemann of Hamburg and, when he declined, to Christoph Graupner of Darmstadt.2 Only when Graupner could not obtain a release from his current position was Bach given the job. He was elected cantor of Leipzig on 22 April 1723. Bach himself regarded the post of cantor of the Thomasschule as inferior to his later court title from the King of Poland and Elector of Saxony.

Was Bach then forgotten until Mendelssohn rescued him? It is conventional to say so, because Mendelssohn conducted the St Matthew Passion in Berlin in 1829. But Mozart and Beethoven had practised Bach's preludes and fugues.3 His sons Carl Philipp Emanuel and Johann Christian, the "London" Bach, kept his legacy alive for a generation after his death, even though they turned away from his contrapuntal style.

One reference work puts it bluntly: it is historically incorrect to maintain that Bach was not appreciated by his contemporaries.4 The 1829 performance mattered, but it revived a reputation that had never quite died.

concepts.title: Mozart: Poison, a Requiem and a Myth
concepts.contentHtml:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, born in Salzburg in 1756, played the keyboard at 3 and composed at 5. In July 1791 he received a commission to compose a Requiem for an anonymous patron, Count von Walsegg, who wished to pass it off as his own. His health was failing, and he died in Vienna on 5 December 1791, leaving the Requiem to be completed by his pupil Süssmayr. The circumstances of his death have given rise to many sensational theories, none proved.1

The most famous is that Antonio Salieri poisoned him. Salieri (1750 to 1825) held the court post of Kapellmeister that Mozart had hoped to win, and the Concise Oxford Dictionary of Music says he was hostile to Mozart, but that there is no truth in the legend that he poisoned him.2 The legend is told in Rimsky-Korsakov's opera Mozart and Salieri. Salieri was also a teacher, and his pupils included Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt.

A modern myth carries Mozart's name too. In 1993 Rauscher and colleagues reported that after 10 minutes of Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos (K. 448), volunteers did better on spatial reasoning tasks than after relaxation instructions or silence,3 scoring 8 and 9 points higher on average. The effect lasted only 10 to 15 minutes, some investigators could not reproduce it,4 and Rauscher stressed that it did not touch general intelligence. Even so, claims of lasting brain boosts, especially for children, fed a small industry selling classical music collections.

The idea then spread into medicine. A 2023 meta-analysis by Sandra Oberleiter and Jakob Pietschnig looked at studies claiming that K. 448 helps people with epilepsy and other conditions. It found trivial to small effects that were not statistically significant,5 from studies with as few as 11 and at most 70 participants. A famous composer does not make weak evidence strong.

concepts.title: What Beethoven Heard
concepts.contentHtml:
A popular belief holds that Ludwig van Beethoven was born deaf. He was not. He was born in Bonn in December 1770, and according to the most cited documents his hearing loss started in 1796 at the age of 26.1 It seems to have begun with high frequencies, and he complained of permanent ringing in the ears (tinnitus) and a loss of sound discrimination. In 1802 he wrote to his brothers the letter now called the Heiligenstadt Testament, describing an incurable malady that had forced him into solitude. From 1818 he relied on conversation books, in which visitors wrote what they wanted to say.2

What caused it? A 2020 systematic review of a century of medical papers counted the diagnoses proposed: otosclerosis, an abnormal bone growth in the ear, ten times; syphilis nine times; Paget's disease of bone six times; and others including lead poisoning, sarcoidosis and lupus. Even 250 years after his birth, the authors concluded, the cause remains unclear.3

Then DNA joined the evidence. In 2023 a team led by Tristan Begg of the University of Cambridge sequenced Beethoven's genome from five matching locks of hair, all from the last seven years of his life and judged almost certainly authentic. A famous lock, said to have been cut from the dead composer's head by the 15-year-old musician Ferdinand Hiller, turned out to come from a woman.4 Earlier tests on that Hiller lock had supported the idea that lead poisoning contributed to his illnesses, including his deafness, so that theory lost its main evidence.

The genome showed that Beethoven was predisposed to liver disease and had a hepatitis B infection, but the team could not find a definitive cause for his deafness.5 Science settled one question about the hair and left the bigger one open.

title: Raga, Gamelan and Maqam
description: Three great musical systems beyond Europe, and what happened when they met the West

concepts.title: Raga: Colour and Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sanskrit word raga comes from a root meaning "colour". In the classical music of India, raga is the combined concept of melody and scale.1 To a listener, a raga is a family of melodies that share key phrases and inflections, a scale, and psychological associations. To a musician, it is a resource of melodic ideas from which to create music that is at once unique and familiar. So two performances of the same raga can sound quite different and still be recognisably the same raga.

A raga comes with rules. Some of the most important describe how it ascends and descends: a note may be left out on the way up and used on the way down, and a line may zigzag, a movement called vakra, "crooked". Indian music does not generally use equal temperament.2 Musicians tend to tune to pure acoustic intervals, closer to what Western theory calls just intonation.

The theory is old and has kept changing. The scholar Bharata, in the Natya Shastra (dated to around the year 200), describes twenty-two microtonal intervals called shruti. In 1661 Venkatamakhi classified the ragas of southern India into seventy-two basic scales. In the north, Bhatkhande (1860 to 1936) organised ragas in terms of ten parent scales called thats, one of which matches the Western major scale.

Then came a famous meeting. The sitarist Ravi Shankar, born in Benares in 1920, had studied for years with his guru Allauddin Khan in the village of Maihar, and had performed with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin in Paris in 1958. In 1966 George Harrison of the Beatles heard one of his albums and arranged to meet him, then spent seven weeks in India learning the sitar.3 Shankar played the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 and Woodstock in 1969, and in 1971 joined Harrison for two sold-out concerts at Madison Square Garden for refugees from Bangladesh.

concepts.title: Gamelan: An Orchestra That Belongs Together
concepts.contentHtml:
The word gamelan refers to a set of instruments from the islands of Java and Bali in Indonesia: tuned gongs, gong chimes (racks of small gongs) and metal-keyed instruments of many sizes. In performance they are joined by drums, xylophones, fiddles, flutes and zithers, as well as singers.1 Each sound has a job. In Javanese gamelan, the stroke of a large hanging gong marks the end of the main musical unit, the gongan, while smaller gongs divide it in order of importance, rather like a clock marking hours, minutes and seconds.

Gamelan tuning does not match the piano. A full Javanese gamelan is really two sets in two tuning systems, and the two sets are never played at the same time.2 Slendro has five notes per octave, separated by short and medium steps. Pelog has seven pitches per octave, but each piece is built on one of three five-note selections, in which narrow and wide steps are clearly heard. The two systems share at least one common tone. A gamelan is treated as an individual: the set at the University of California, Riverside is named Kyai Telaga Semu,3 "Venerable Lake of Illusions".

Western composers met gamelan at the world's fairs. At the 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris, Claude Debussy first encountered the music of a Javanese gamelan ensemble.4 A recent analysis calls it a pivotal moment for his mature style, most clearly heard in his 1903 piano piece "Pagodes", the first of the Estampes.

Is gamelan then utterly unlike other music? A 2023 study of a large cross-cultural database of scales found that the similarities between societies are more striking than the differences: the steps between notes fall between 100 and 400 cents (a semitone is 100), and most scales are close to evenly spaced five-note or seven-note patterns.5 Gamelan tuning is distinctive, but it sits inside a wider human pattern.

concepts.title: Maqam, the Oud and the Cairo Congress
concepts.contentHtml:
Much Arab and Turkish music is built on maqam (Turkish makam), a system of melodic modes, each with its own scale and habits. One of its central instruments, the plucked oud, also gave Europe a word: lute comes, through French and Provençal, from the Arabic al-'ud. The European lute, with its distinct neck and central soundhole, took shape probably in Spain in the 14th century.1

In the spring of 1932, under King Fuad I of Egypt, Cairo hosted the first Congress of Arab Music, gathering Egyptian, Arab and European musicologists and composers, among them Béla Bartók. At the outset it was called a congress of Oriental music. During the meeting it was agreed to call it the Arab Music Congress,2 because delegates were trying to define a new music, Arab music, after separating from the Ottoman Empire.

One question ran through the debates: is there such a thing as an Arabic scale, and is it the same as the Turkish one? The discussions convinced participants that the scales were not the same: some degrees differ slightly, notably notes that produce intervals that can roughly be described as quarter tones,3 half the size of the step between neighbouring piano keys. Sources disagree on how long the congress lasted: the French national library dates it from 28 March to 3 April, while a scholar of the congress speaks of three weeks.

The congress also treated the gramophone as a research tool. A recording commission had 342 pieces recorded on 78 rpm discs by Gramophone (His Master's Voice), never published at the time;4 copies went to the British Library and Berlin's Phonogrammarchiv among others. The proceedings were published in 1933 to 1934, but the recordings were only made available in 2015, some 80 years later.5

title: The Recording Revolution
description: From soot tracings and tinfoil to the first jazz record, hip hop, MIDI and the data of the charts

concepts.title: The Voice That Wrote Itself
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask who invented sound recording and most people say Thomas Edison. But Edison was not the first person to record sound.1 In 1857 a French inventor, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, devised the phonautograph: a horn and a stylus that traced the vibrations of sound in an exceedingly thin layer of lampblack (soot) on glass or paper. Scott did not intend his tracings to be played back; that concept was another 20 years away. He hoped they would become a kind of natural shorthand that could be read by eye.

In 1860 Scott made a number of recordings: he sang songs and recited poetry and plays in several languages, with a tuning fork tracing its own vibrations beside the voice so that time could be measured by counting its squiggles. The papers sat in French archives for almost 150 years. In 2008 the American group First Sounds found and played back recordings he had made in Paris in 1860, humanity's first recordings of its own voice.2

Edison's aim was different: recordings that a machine could play back. In 1877 his team pressed a needle against a strip of waxed paper while Edison spoke "Mary had a little lamb", a stock phrase for testing telephones. Pulled through again, the strip gave back "ary ad elll am": not fine talking, his assistant Charles Batchelor recalled, but the shape of it was there.3 Late in November sketches were drawn for a phonograph that recorded on tinfoil wrapped around a revolving cylinder,4 and on 7 December 1877 Edison demonstrated it to the editors of Scientific American in New York.

One more twist: just weeks before Edison first expressed his idea, the Parisian Charles Cros had written down a proposal to play back sound, but he never built a machine. So the honest answer to the opening question has two parts. Scott first recorded sound; Edison was the first to play it back.5

concepts.title: From the Balafon to the Electric Guitar
concepts.contentHtml:
Long before recording, West Africa had professional keepers of musical memory, the jeliw or griots, whom you met in African Kingdoms performing the epic of Sundiata. Their instruments carry history too. The Sosso-Bala, a sacred balafon (a wooden xylophone), is said to have belonged to King Sumaoro Kanté, who took the throne of Sosso in the early thirteenth century. The original is still kept in a round mud hut in the village of Nyagassola in northern Guinea by the Kouyaté griots,1 and only their patriarch may play it on important occasions.

The 21-string kora, a harp, is younger than its fame suggests. The ethnomusicologist Eric Charry writes that the kora has origins in the Kaabu federation of the Senegambian Mandinka in the 1700s,2 while widespread oral traditions place its birth at Sanementereng on the Gambian coast. Across the Atlantic, the banjo is probably of African origin, taken to the United States by enslaved people.3 Rural African American work songs carried the bent or "blue" notes that lie outside the standard scale, the notes that came to characterise the blues.

Recording then shaped who got heard. The record generally acknowledged as the first jazz recording, "Livery Stable Blues" by the Original Dixieland Jass Band in 1917, was a best-seller for Victor but is a problematic first: it was a white band performing an African American genre,4 and its members claimed to have invented jazz instead of crediting the New Orleans musicians they had learned from.

The electric guitar, invented in the 1930s, added amplified sustain. One of its early stars was not a rock singer but a gospel singer, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, whose style developed from the 1930s to the 1960s and influenced Chuck Berry, Eric Clapton and Keith Richards.5

concepts.title: Breakbeats, MIDI and Music as Data
concepts.contentHtml:
On 11 August 1973, an 18-year-old Jamaican-American DJ, Clive Campbell, known as DJ Kool Herc, threw a back-to-school party for his sister Cindy in the rec room at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the South Bronx.1 Using two turntables and two copies of the same record, he stretched out a song's break, its percussive instrumental stretch, and talked over it while dancers improvised. Hip hop grew from those breaks into a culture of MCing (rap), DJing, breaking and graffiti.

Machines learned to talk to each other too. In June 1981 Ikutaro Kakehashi, president of Roland, approached Tom Oberheim about an industry standard for connecting synthesisers.2 Dave Smith of Sequential Circuits proposed a Universal Synthesizer Interface that October. The Japanese companies suggested the name UMI, and Smith countered with MIDI, the Musical Instrument Digital Interface, which lets a keyboard from one maker play a synthesiser or computer from another. The MP3, whose maths you met in Fourier Analysis, got its name on 14 July 1995 through an internal email poll at Fraunhofer IIS;3 its developers had struggled with Suzanne Vega's unaccompanied song "Tom's Diner".

Recordings also turned music history into data. In 2015 Matthias Mauch and colleagues analysed about 17,000 songs from the US Billboard Hot 100 between 1960 and 2010. Pop evolved continuously, but fastest in three stylistic revolutions, around 1964, 1983 and 1991.4

The popular story says the Beatles and the British Invasion transformed American pop in 1964. The data are more modest: the changes began well before the British Invasion started in late 1963,5 and acts such as the Beatles and the Rolling Stones exaggerated trends that were already under way. The largest revolution of the three was 1991, when rap-related styles expanded at the expense of rock.6
